# S1M-1 Unit 0: Introduction to Psychological Research Methods

## Unit 0: Introduction to Psychological Research Methods

> From the AP Psychology Midterm review guide. Range: Unit 0 (Research Methods), Unit 1 (Biological Bases of Behavior), Modules 1.5 Consciousness & Sleep, 1.6 Sensation, 2.1 Perception, 2.2 Thinking, Problem-Solving & Creativity. Student-made reference material: where it differs from class, follow class.

## 1.1 The Scientific Attitude

Critical thinking in psychology rests on three habits working together: curiosity, skepticism, and humility. Together they let you examine assumptions, appraise sources, discern hidden biases, and weigh evidence against conclusions. Three biases constantly get in the way: hindsight bias (the "I knew it all along" effect), overconfidence in our own judgments, and the tendency to perceive order in genuinely random events.

## 1.2 Key Concepts

- **Falsifiability.** A scientific claim must be testable. The classic non-falsifiable example: the existence of God.
- **Operational definition.** A precise, measurable definition of a research procedure or concept.

- **Hypothesis vs. theory.** A hypothesis is a testable prediction; a theory is an organized explanation. A hypothesis is often implied by a theory.

## 1.3 Non-Experimental Methods

- **Case study.** In-depth analysis of one individual or group.
- **Naturalistic observation.** Observing behavior without interfering.

- **Survey.** Self-report via questions.
- **Correlational study.** Measuring the association between two variables.

**Exam note.** Know the three survey biases: wording effect, social desirability bias, and self-report bias (people report their own behavior inaccurately).

- **Random sampling.** Everyone in the population has an EQUAL CHANCE of being selected.

**Exam note.** On the exam, write "equal chance" — the phrase "random" alone does not earn the point.

Population refers to ALL those studied; the sample is the SOME who represent the population.

## 1.4 Correlation

A correlation is a linear association between two variables, summarized by the correlation coefficient r, which ranges from −1.00 to +1.00. Correlational data are displayed in scatterplots — the only graph type you need to know for the exam. Two related pitfalls: an illusory correlation is perceiving a relationship that is not actually there (similar to confirmation bias), and regression toward the mean describes how extreme scores drift toward the average on retest.

**Exam note.** r is NOT the slope. The sign of r only tells you the direction of the relationship.

**Exam note.** Illusory correlation, lurking variables, and "correlation ≠ causation" are three distinct concepts — do not blur them together.

![Scatterplots: r = +0.9, r = −0.9, and r = 0. The coefficient's sign gives direction only — it is not the slope.](/media/pa-guides/ap-psychology/s1m-fig-01.png)

*Figure 1. Scatterplots: r = +0.9, r = −0.9, and r = 0. The coefficient's sign gives direction only — it is not the slope.*

## 1.5 Experimentation

An experiment compares an experimental group against a control group. Random assignment equalizes pre-existing differences between the groups. In a single-blind study participants are blind to the treatment; in a double-blind study participants AND researchers are blind. Key vocabulary: the placebo effect (improvement from expectation alone), confounding variables (factors that may influence the dependent variable), and experimenter bias (researcher expectations skewing results). The independent variable is what the researcher manipulates; the dependent variable is what is measured.

| **Validity** | **Reliability** |
|---|---|
| Does the experiment measure what it is supposed to measure? | Can the results be consistently replicated? |

**Exam note.** Reliability cannot be inferred from the name alone — memorize the definition: consistently replicated.

## 1.6 Other Research Methods and Ethics

- **Developmental designs.** Twin studies (identical vs. fraternal twins), cross-sectional, and longitudinal studies.
- **Data types.** Quantitative vs. qualitative (categorical) research.

- **Ethics.** Informed consent — informed ASSENT for minors — debriefing, protection from greater-than-usual harm, and confidentiality.
- **Guidelines.** Issued by the APA and BPS; animal studies are governed by common sense.

## 1.7 Statistics

Descriptive statistics measure and describe characteristics (in AP Psychology, histograms are basically bar charts). Inferential statistics ask whether results can generalize to the larger population. Better studies have representative rather than biased samples, bigger rather than smaller samples, more estimates rather than fewer, and may pool findings in a meta-analysis.

| **Mode** | **Median** | **Mean** |
|---|---|---|
| Most frequent value. Bimodal = two peaks (textbook-tested, not covered in class). | Middle value. | Average — pulled toward the tail in skewed data. |

Measures of variation include the range and the standard deviation (skip the IQR).

**Exam note.** Define standard deviation as the AVERAGE distance of all data points from the mean.

Skew: look at the tail. A tail trailing right = right (positive) skew, and the mean is HIGHEST in positive skew — the reverse for negative skew.

![Distributions in negative skew (mean lowest), normal (mean = median), and positive skew (mean highest). Always read the tail.](/media/pa-guides/ap-psychology/s1m-fig-02.png)

*Figure 2. Distributions in negative skew (mean lowest), normal (mean = median), and positive skew (mean highest). Always read the tail.*

The normal curve is bell-shaped, and the 68-95-99.7 rule gives the percentage of scores within 1, 2, and 3 standard deviations of the mean.

![The normal curve: 68% of scores fall within ±1 SD, 95% within ±2 SD, and 99.7% within ±3 SD of the mean.](/media/pa-guides/ap-psychology/s1m-fig-03.png)

*Figure 3. The normal curve: 68% of scores fall within ±1 SD, 95% within ±2 SD, and 99.7% within ±3 SD of the mean.*

## 1.8 Statistical Significance

A p-value tells you how likely the result occurred by chance, assuming there is no difference in the population.

**Exam note.** In AP Psychology, p < 0.05 AND p = 0.05 both mean "no difference" (no significant effect).

Statistical significance is not the same as practical significance; the effect size tells you the strength of the relationship between two variables.

# S1M-2 Unit 1: Biological Bases of Behavior

## Unit 1: Biological Bases of Behavior

> From the AP Psychology Midterm review guide. Range: Unit 0 (Research Methods), Unit 1 (Biological Bases of Behavior), Modules 1.5 Consciousness & Sleep, 1.6 Sensation, 2.1 Perception, 2.2 Thinking, Problem-Solving & Creativity. Student-made reference material: where it differs from class, follow class.

## 2.1 Nature vs. Nurture

Nature covers natural selection and evolutionary psychology; nurture covers environment and heredity.

**Exam note.** "50% genetic" means 50% of the INDIVIDUAL DIFFERENCES in the trait — not 50% of your height.

Identical vs. fraternal twins form the basis of twin studies.

## 2.2 The Nervous System

| **Part** | **Contents** |
|---|---|
| CNS (central) | Brain + spinal cord. Bundles of axons = TRACTS; clusters of soma = NUCLEI. |
| PNS (peripheral) | Everything outside the CNS. Bundles = NERVES; clusters = GANGLIA. |
| PNS branches | Somatic = voluntary. Autonomic = automatic: sympathetic (arousal) vs. parasympathetic (calm). |

**Exam note.** CNS terms are tracts and nuclei; PNS terms are nerves and ganglia. Exam questions may use them without defining them (the optic nerve is a named exception).

Sensory neurons carry input; motor neurons carry output. The reflex arc runs: sensory neuron → INTERNeuron → motor neuron.

## 2.3 The Neuron

Know the parts: soma, dendrites, axon, myelin sheath, node of Ranvier, axon hillock, and axon terminal. Glial cells support neurons; Schwann cells produce myelin in the PNS.

**Exam note.** If you are labeling a CNS neuron, do NOT write "Schwann cell" — write "glial cell" (oligodendrocyte earns bonus-level credit).

The action potential: resting potential −70 mV, threshold −55 mV; the response is all-or-none, followed by a refractory period. The sequence is depolarization → repolarization → hyperpolarization.

![The action potential: resting potential −70 mV, threshold −55 mV, all-or-none firing, refractory period.](/media/pa-guides/ap-psychology/s1m-fig-04.png)

*Figure 4. The action potential: resting potential −70 mV, threshold −55 mV, all-or-none firing, refractory period.*

## 2.4 Neural Communication

At the synaptic cleft, neurotransmitters are released from the pre-synaptic axon terminal...

**Exam note.** ...and they BIND receptors on the post-synaptic neuron. Never write that neurotransmitters GO INTO the post-synaptic neuron.

Signals are excitatory or inhibitory; reuptake recycles neurotransmitters back into the sending neuron.

## 2.5 Neurotransmitters

| **Neurotransmitter** | **Role** | **Linked to** |
|---|---|---|
| Acetylcholine (ACh) | Muscle action, learning, memory | Alzheimer's disease |
| Dopamine | Movement, learning, attention, emotion | Schizophrenia, Parkinson's |
| Serotonin | Mood, hunger, sleep, arousal | Depression |
| Norepinephrine | Alertness, arousal, mood | — |
| GABA | MAJOR inhibitory | Undersupply: seizures, tremors, insomnia |
| Glutamate | MAJOR excitatory; memory | Migraines, seizures |
| Endorphins | Pain & pleasure perception | — |
| Substance P | Pain perception, immune response | — |

**Exam note.** If the question says adrenaline or noradrenaline, it means the HORMONE. Norepinephrine is the neurotransmitter.

Agonists enhance a neurotransmitter's activity; antagonists block it. Reuptake inhibitors such as SSRIs act as agonists.

## 2.6 The Endocrine System and Drugs

Hormones travel via glands — know the adrenal gland and pituitary gland, and the hormone oxytocin.

| **Class** | **Examples** |
|---|---|
| Depressants | Alcohol, barbiturates, opioids |
| Stimulants | Nicotine, cocaine, methamphetamine, MDMA (ecstasy) |
| Hallucinogens | LSD, MDMA, marijuana |

Substance use disorder: addiction vs. tolerance (needing more of the drug for the same effect).

## 2.7 Studying the Brain

- **Approaches.** Biopsychosocial approach (at most 1 MCQ); neuroplasticity; lesion studies.
- **Imaging.** Structural: MRI, CT. Functional: EEG, MEG, PET, fMRI.

## 2.8 Brain Structures and Functions

| **Structure** | **Function** |
|---|---|
| Brainstem (medulla + pons + midbrain) | Life-support basics; the medulla and pons are parts OF the brainstem, not separate from it. |
| Reticular formation | Arousal |
| Thalamus | Sensory relay to cortex |
| Hypothalamus | Homeostasis; talks to the endocrine system via the pituitary; reward center |
| Cerebellum | Balance, coordination |
| Amygdala | Emotion (fear) |
| Hippocampus | Memory |
| Cerebral cortex | Outer grey matter OF the cerebrum |

## 2.9 The Cerebral Cortex

Four lobes: frontal, parietal, occipital, temporal. The motor cortex sits at the rear of the frontal lobe; the somatosensory cortex in the parietal lobe; association areas fill the rest. One odd fact: the right temporal lobe also handles facial recognition.

- **Language.** Broca's area (production) and Wernicke's area (comprehension) — BOTH on the LEFT hemisphere.
- **Contralateral organization.** Each side of the brain connects to the body's opposite side.

- **Hemisphere specialties.** Left: language, logic, analytical. Right: music & art, visual-spatial, creativity.

## 2.10 Classic Case Studies

- **Phineas Gage.** Frontal lobe damage → personality change.
- **Neurogenesis.** Forming new neurons.

- **Split-brain.** Corpus callosum severed. Right visual field → the person can SAY what they saw; left visual field → the LEFT HAND picks the object (contralateral processing).

**Exam note.** If you can explain split-brain studies, you understand how the brain works — a top exam favorite.

# S1M-3 Module 1.5: Consciousness and Sleep

## Module 1.5: Consciousness and Sleep

> From the AP Psychology Midterm review guide. Range: Unit 0 (Research Methods), Unit 1 (Biological Bases of Behavior), Modules 1.5 Consciousness & Sleep, 1.6 Sensation, 2.1 Perception, 2.2 Thinking, Problem-Solving & Creativity. Student-made reference material: where it differs from class, follow class.

## 3.1 Consciousness and Dual Processing

Consciousness is being aware of yourself and your surroundings; it has multiple states — awake, asleep, dreaming. Cognitive neuroscience studies how brain activity connects to mental processes.

Thinking, knowing, remembering, and communicating happen on two levels at the same time: the conscious track is slow, deliberate, and step-by-step (like long division), while the unconscious track is fast, automatic, and effortless (like catching a ball).

- **Blindsight.** The eyes work but the part of the brain that makes you "aware" of seeing is damaged — a person responds to visual things without being consciously aware of them. Lawrence Weiskrantz walked a blindsight patient down a cluttered hallway; told it was empty, the patient had no idea obstacles existed — yet weaved around every one.
- **Parallel processing.** The brain handles many parts of a stimulus at once (recognizing a friend's face = color + shape + movement together).

- **Sequential processing.** Handling one part at a time, step by step — used for new or difficult problems.

## 3.2 Sleep and the Circadian Rhythm

Sleep is a natural, repeating loss of consciousness — NOT the same as a coma, general anesthesia (drugs that make you unconscious for surgery), or hibernation.

- **Circadian rhythm.** Your internal biological clock on a roughly 24-hour cycle ("about a day" in Latin), controlling sleep, body temperature, alertness, and hunger.
- **The master clock.** The suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN): light → SCN decreases melatonin (the "sleepy hormone") → you wake up.

- **Desynchronization.** Internal clock vs. outside world out of sync (jet lag).

![The circadian rhythm over 24 hours: body temperature, alertness, and melatonin, set by the suprachiasmatic nucleus.](/media/pa-guides/ap-psychology/s1m-fig-05.png)

*Figure 5. The circadian rhythm over 24 hours: body temperature, alertness, and melatonin, set by the suprachiasmatic nucleus.*

## 3.3 The Stages of Sleep

Brain wave signatures follow a sequence: beta (alert) → alpha (relaxed) → theta (Stage 1) → delta (Stage 3 deep) → REM (rapid, irregular).

![Brain wave signatures: beta, alpha, theta, delta, and REM.](/media/pa-guides/ap-psychology/s1m-fig-06.png)

*Figure 6. Brain wave signatures: beta, alpha, theta, delta, and REM.*

| **Stage** | **Brain activity** | **Key facts** |
|---|---|---|
| Awake (relaxed) | Alpha waves — slow, big waves | Drowsy, calm |
| Awake (alert) | Beta waves — fast, small waves | Thinking, focused |
| NREM-1 | Theta waves | Hallucinations (seeing/hearing things that aren't there); hypnagogic sensations = hallucinations right as you fall asleep (the falling feeling) |
| NREM-2 | Sleep spindles (short bursts of fast brain activity) | Spindles help process and store memories |
| NREM-3 (deep) | Delta waves — large, slow waves | Hardest to wake; the body restores itself |
| REM | Rapid, irregular waves (like Stage 1) BUT heart rate rises, breathing fast & irregular | Dreams happen here; paradoxical sleep (brain active, body paralyzed); REM rebound = extra REM after deprivation |

Across a night of sleep, deep sleep dominates early and REM periods grow longer toward morning.

![A night of sleep in young vs. older adults: deep sleep early, lengthening REM periods toward morning.](/media/pa-guides/ap-psychology/s1m-fig-07.png)

*Figure 7. A night of sleep in young vs. older adults: deep sleep early, lengthening REM periods toward morning.*

## 3.4 Why We Sleep

Six reasons: (1) protects — kept ancestors safe from nighttime dangers; (2) restores — repairs body and brain; (3) consolidates memory — files away what you learned; (4) feeds creative thinking — the brain connects ideas; (5) supports growth — growth hormone is released; (6) conserves energy.

Sleep deprivation causes: fatigue, irritability, poor concentration, weak memory, depression, obesity, joint inflammation, slowed performance, and a weakened immune system.

## 3.5 Sleep Disorders

- **Insomnia (in- = not; somnus = sleep).** Trouble falling or staying asleep.
- **Narcolepsy (narco = sleep).** Sudden, uncontrollable sleep attacks during the day.

- **Sleep apnea (apnea = "no breathing").** Repeatedly stopping breathing during sleep.

## 3.6 Why Do We Dream? (Four Theories)

- **1. Information processing.** Dreams sort and file memories.
- **2. Physiological function.** Dreams exercise brain circuits.

- **3. Neural activation.** Random brain firing turned into stories.
- **4. Cognitive development.** Dreaming helps the brain develop.

# S1M-4 Module 1.6: Sensation

## Module 1.6: Sensation

> From the AP Psychology Midterm review guide. Range: Unit 0 (Research Methods), Unit 1 (Biological Bases of Behavior), Modules 1.5 Consciousness & Sleep, 1.6 Sensation, 2.1 Perception, 2.2 Thinking, Problem-Solving & Creativity. Student-made reference material: where it differs from class, follow class.

## 4.1 Foundations

- **Sensation.** Detecting raw information from the environment (light, sound, pressure).
- **Sensory receptor.** A cell that detects a specific type of energy (light, sound waves, chemicals).

- **Transduction (trans- = across; ducere = to lead).** Converting sensory energy into neural signals the brain can read. Three steps: receive → transform → deliver.
- **Bottom-up processing.** The brain builds perception from raw sensory data, starting with the senses.

- **Top-down processing.** Interpreting sensations using expectations and memory, starting with what you already know.
- **Psychophysics.** The study of how physical stimuli relate to what we mentally experience.

## 4.2 Thresholds and Key Terms

| **Concept** | **Meaning** | **Example** |
|---|---|---|
| Absolute threshold | Smallest amount of a stimulus you can detect 50% of the time | A candle flame seen 30 miles away on a dark night |
| Difference threshold (JND) | Smallest difference between two stimuli you can detect | Noticing your phone got slightly heavier with a new case |
| Weber's Law | JND is a constant percentage of the original stimulus | +1 candle is obvious with 10 candles, invisible with 100 |
| Signal detection theory | Detection depends on signal strength AND your expectations/alertness | A sleepy parent hears the baby; a partygoer doesn't |
| Subliminal | Too weak for conscious awareness | An image flashed too briefly to "see" |
| Sensory adaptation | Receptors get used to a constant stimulus — you stop noticing it | You stop smelling your own house |

![Weber's Law: the just-noticeable difference grows in constant proportion to the stimulus.](/media/pa-guides/ap-psychology/s1m-fig-08.png)

*Figure 8. Weber's Law: the just-noticeable difference grows in constant proportion to the stimulus.*

## 4.3 Vision

Light is energy. Wavelength determines hue (the color you see); amplitude determines intensity (brightness).

Light path through the eye: cornea → pupil → lens → retina → optic nerve. The lens changes shape to focus (accommodation).

![Anatomy of the eye: cornea, pupil, iris, lens, retina, fovea, blind spot, and optic nerve.](/media/pa-guides/ap-psychology/s1m-fig-09.png)

*Figure 9. Anatomy of the eye: cornea, pupil, iris, lens, retina, fovea, blind spot, and optic nerve.*

|  | **Rods** | **Cones** |
|---|---|---|
| Detect | Black/white, dim light | Color and fine detail |
| Where | Edges of the retina | Clustered at the fovea (center) |
| Signal path | Photoreceptors → bipolar cells → ganglion cells → optic nerve | Same; fibers cross at the optic chiasm |

![Retinal processing: light triggers rods and cones, which activate bipolar cells, then ganglion cells, whose axons form the optic nerve.](/media/pa-guides/ap-psychology/s1m-fig-10.png)

*Figure 10. Retinal processing: light triggers rods and cones, which activate bipolar cells, then ganglion cells, whose axons form the optic nerve.*

- **Blind spot.** Where the optic nerve exits — no receptors there, so you can't see it (your brain paints over it).
- **Trichromatic theory (tri = three).** Three cone types (red, green, blue) mix to make all colors.

- **Opponent-process theory.** Cells work in opposing pairs (red vs. green, blue vs. yellow) — explains afterimages.

Both color theories are correct: they describe different stages of processing.

![Trichromatic theory (three cone types mix) vs. opponent-process theory (opposing cell pairs).](/media/pa-guides/ap-psychology/s1m-fig-11.png)

*Figure 11. Trichromatic theory (three cone types mix) vs. opponent-process theory (opposing cell pairs).*

- **Feature detectors.** Brain cells that fire only for specific features (edges, lines, movement); the brain combines them with parallel processing.

## 4.4 Audition (Hearing)

Frequency (waves per second) determines pitch (how high or low); amplitude determines loudness, measured in decibels (dB).

![Frequency → pitch; amplitude → loudness.](/media/pa-guides/ap-psychology/s1m-fig-12.png)

*Figure 12. Frequency → pitch; amplitude → loudness.*

Sound path: pinna → eardrum → hammer/anvil/stirrup → oval window → cochlea → hair cells bend → auditory nerve.

![Anatomy of the ear: outer, middle (ossicles), and inner ear (cochlea, hair cells, auditory nerve).](/media/pa-guides/ap-psychology/s1m-fig-13.png)

*Figure 13. Anatomy of the ear: outer, middle (ossicles), and inner ear (cochlea, hair cells, auditory nerve).*

| **Conductive hearing loss** | **Sensorineural hearing loss** |
|---|---|
| Problem in the mechanical parts (eardrum, ossicles) — sound can't get through | Damage to the cochlea or auditory nerve — the signal never becomes neural (loud noise kills hair cells; causes tinnitus) |

- **Place theory.** Explains high pitches — different spots on the basilar membrane vibrate.
- **Frequency theory.** Explains low pitches — hair cells fire at the same rate as the wave.

- **Loudness.** How many hair cells fire.
- **Stereophonic hearing (stereo = 3D).** Comparing the ears to locate sound.

Decibels are logarithmic: each +10 dB is roughly 10× the intensity.

![The decibel scale is logarithmic: each +10 dB represents a tenfold increase in intensity.](/media/pa-guides/ap-psychology/s1m-fig-14.png)

*Figure 14. The decibel scale is logarithmic: each +10 dB represents a tenfold increase in intensity.*

## 4.5 Touch and Pain

Skin detects pressure, warmth, cold, and pain — with separate receptors for each. Nociceptors (noci = harm) are pain receptors.

- **Gate-control theory.** Rubbing an injury floods the spinal "gate" with touch signals, so the pain signal is blocked. Endorphins are the body's own painkillers.
- **Phantom limb sensation.** Feeling an itch or pain in a missing limb — the brain generates the feeling.

- **Tinnitus.** Ringing in the ears with no external sound.

Pain can be controlled by placebos (fake treatments that work because you believe), distraction, and social/cultural factors — pain is part perception.

![Gate-control theory: touch signals (rubbing) close the spinal gate on pain signals; endorphins also close the gate.](/media/pa-guides/ap-psychology/s1m-fig-15.png)

*Figure 15. Gate-control theory: touch signals (rubbing) close the spinal gate on pain signals; endorphins also close the gate.*

## 4.6 Taste and Smell

| **Taste (gustation)** | **Smell (olfaction)** |
|---|---|
| 6 basic tastes: sweet, sour, salty, bitter, umami (savory), oleogustus (fatty) | Path: odor → receptor cells in the olfactory membrane → olfactory bulb → olfactory nerve → brain |
| Taster types: supertasters (many taste buds — find veggies bitter), medium, non-tasters | The only sense that skips the thalamus — it goes straight to emotion & memory areas (why smells trigger vivid memories) |
|  | Pheromones = airborne chemical signals between members of a species |

## 4.7 Body Senses and Interaction

| **Sense** | **What it is** | **Receptor** |
|---|---|---|
| Kinesthesis (kine = movement) | Knowing where body parts are without looking | Proprioceptors in joints, tendons, muscles |
| Vestibular sense | Balance and head position | Semicircular canals + vestibular sacs (fluid in the inner ear) |

- **Sensory interaction.** Senses influence each other. McGurk effect: watch lips say "ga" while hearing "ba" → you hear "da".
- **Embodied cognition.** The body influences the mind: sit on a hard chair → judge criminals as "hard on crime."

- **Synesthesia (syn = together).** Senses cross-wired — some people see music as colors or taste words.

# S1M-5 Module 2.1: Perception

## Module 2.1: Perception

> From the AP Psychology Midterm review guide. Range: Unit 0 (Research Methods), Unit 1 (Biological Bases of Behavior), Modules 1.5 Consciousness & Sleep, 1.6 Sensation, 2.1 Perception, 2.2 Thinking, Problem-Solving & Creativity. Student-made reference material: where it differs from class, follow class.

## 5.1 Attention

Perception is the brain organizing and interpreting sensory information. Attention selects what gets processed.

- **Selective attention.** Focusing on one thing while ignoring everything else.
- **Cocktail party effect.** Tuning out a noisy room but instantly hearing your name.

- **Inattentional blindness.** Missing something obvious because attention is elsewhere (the invisible gorilla experiment).
- **Change blindness.** Failing to notice a change in a scene (the person you're talking to gets swapped).

- **Perceptual set.** Expectations shape what you perceive (top-down) — expect danger, and a stick looks like a snake.

## 5.2 Gestalt Organization

Gestalt (German for "shape/form") means the whole is more than the sum of its parts — the brain auto-organizes what it sees.

Grouping principles: proximity, similarity, closure, continuity.

- **Figure-ground.** Separating the object (figure) from the background (ground) — the vase/faces illusion.

![Gestalt grouping principles: proximity, similarity, closure, continuity.](/media/pa-guides/ap-psychology/s1m-fig-16.png)

*Figure 16. Gestalt grouping principles: proximity, similarity, closure, continuity.*

## 5.3 Depth Perception

Depth perception is seeing in 3D. The visual cliff experiment showed babies avoid the "deep" side of a glass table — depth perception is partly innate.

- **Binocular cues (need both eyes).** Retinal disparity & convergence.

![Binocular cues: retinal disparity (near objects produce a bigger difference between the two eyes' images) and convergence (eyes angle inward for near objects).](/media/pa-guides/ap-psychology/s1m-fig-17.png)

*Figure 17. Binocular cues: retinal disparity (near objects produce a bigger difference between the two eyes' images) and convergence (eyes angle inward for near objects).*

- **Monocular cues (one eye is enough).** Linear perspective, interposition, texture gradient.

![Monocular depth cues: relative clarity, relative size, texture gradient, linear perspective, and interposition.](/media/pa-guides/ap-psychology/s1m-fig-18.png)

*Figure 18. Monocular depth cues: relative clarity, relative size, texture gradient, linear perspective, and interposition.*

## 5.4 Motion Perception

| **Illusion** | **What tricks you** | **Example** |
|---|---|---|
| Stroboscopic movement | Rapid still frames read as motion | Movies, animation (24 frames/sec) |
| Phi phenomenon | Lights blinking in sequence = one light moving | Neon signs, runway lights |
| Autokinetic effect | A stationary dot in the dark appears to drift | Staring at a single star |

## 5.5 Perceptual Constancy

Perceptual constancy means perceiving objects as stable even as the raw image changes.

- **Color/brightness constancy.** White looks white in sun or candlelight, judged by relative luminance (light reflected compared to surroundings).
- **Shape constancy.** A door still looks rectangular when its image is a trapezoid.

- **Size constancy.** Friends don't shrink as they walk away.

The moon illusion: the horizon moon and the overhead moon have the same retinal size, but context cues near the horizon trick size constancy.

![The moon illusion: context cues near the horizon make the moon look huge; it is the same size overhead.](/media/pa-guides/ap-psychology/s1m-fig-19.png)

*Figure 19. The moon illusion: context cues near the horizon make the moon look huge; it is the same size overhead.*

## 5.6 Critical Period and Perceptual Adaptation

- **Critical period.** An early window when the brain must receive sensory input or perception never develops properly (restored-vision adults can't learn to see faces well).
- **Perceptual adaptation.** The brain adjusts to changed input (upside-down goggles start looking normal after days).

Bottom line: your brain CONSTRUCTS your perceptions.

# S1M-6 Module 2.2: Thinking, Problem-Solving, and Creativity

## Module 2.2: Thinking, Problem-Solving, and Creativity

> From the AP Psychology Midterm review guide. Range: Unit 0 (Research Methods), Unit 1 (Biological Bases of Behavior), Modules 1.5 Consciousness & Sleep, 1.6 Sensation, 2.1 Perception, 2.2 Thinking, Problem-Solving & Creativity. Student-made reference material: where it differs from class, follow class.

## 6.1 Concepts and Schemas

- **Concept.** A mental category of similar things ("bird," "furniture").
- **Prototype.** The most typical example of a concept (a robin is a better "bird" than a penguin).

- **Schema.** A mental framework that organizes knowledge.
- **Assimilate.** Fit new info into an existing schema (wolf → "big dog!").

- **Accommodate.** Change the schema itself (learning wolves are their own category).
- **Metacognition (meta = about).** Thinking about your own thinking.

## 6.2 Creativity

Creativity produces ideas that are both new and valuable.

| **Convergent thinking** | **Divergent thinking** |
|---|---|
| Narrows to one correct answer (standard tests) | Expands to many possible answers ("uses for a brick?") |

Five components of creativity: Expertise, Imaginative thinking, a Venturesome personality, Intrinsic motivation (doing it for its own sake), and a creative Environment. Mnemonic: "Every Idea Ventures If Encouraged."

Obstacles: fixation (getting stuck on one approach) and functional fixedness (only seeing an object's usual use — the candle box as a shelf).

## 6.3 Problem-Solving

| **Strategy** | **How it works** | **Trade-off** |
|---|---|---|
| Algorithm | Step-by-step rule that guarantees the answer | Slow but certain |
| Heuristic | Mental shortcut, rule of thumb | Fast but can mislead |
| Executive functions | The brain's "CEO" — planning, focusing, switching | Fatigues without sleep |
| Insight | Sudden "Aha!" — the answer clicks at once | Can't be forced |

Classic insight puzzle: connect 9 dots with 4 straight lines — impossible until the lines go outside the box ("think outside the box").

## 6.4 Decision Traps

| **Bias** | **Definition** | **Everyday example** |
|---|---|---|
| Confirmation bias | Seek only evidence that supports your belief | Only reading news that agrees with you |
| Mental set | Solve problems the same old way | Restarting the router the same way every time |
| Representativeness heuristic | Judge by stereotypes, ignoring real odds | "Poetry lover = librarian" (salespeople vastly outnumber librarians) |
| Availability heuristic | Judge likelihood by how easily examples come to mind | Fearing planes after one crash story |
| Overconfidence | Overestimate how right you are | "I'm 99% sure I'll finish Friday" |
| Belief perseverance | Cling to beliefs even after they're disproven | Still believing a debunked rumor |
| Framing | Same facts, different wording → different choice | "90% survival" vs "10% mortality" |
| Anchoring bias | First number heard skews your estimate | "Was Gandhi older than 114?" — guess creeps up |

In short: heuristics make us fast; biases make us wrong.

# S1M-7 Exam Pitfalls and Rapid Self-Check

## Exam Pitfalls and Rapid Self-Check

> From the AP Psychology Midterm review guide. Range: Unit 0 (Research Methods), Unit 1 (Biological Bases of Behavior), Modules 1.5 Consciousness & Sleep, 1.6 Sensation, 2.1 Perception, 2.2 Thinking, Problem-Solving & Creativity. Student-made reference material: where it differs from class, follow class.

## Appendix A — Consolidated Exam Pitfalls

The traps below are the ones most likely to cost points. Each is phrased the way you should remember it for the exam.

| **Topic** | **The trap** |
|---|---|
| Random sampling | Write "equal chance," not just "random". |
| Correlation coefficient | Sign = direction only, NOT the slope (range −1.00 to +1.00). |
| Illusory correlation | Not the same as lurking variables or "correlation ≠ causation" — three separate concepts. |
| p-value | p < 0.05 AND p = 0.05 both mean "no difference" in AP Psychology. |
| Significance | Statistical ≠ practical significance — add effect size. |
| Skew | Look at the TAIL; the mean is highest in positive (right) skew. |
| Nervous system terms | CNS = tracts & nuclei; PNS = nerves & ganglia. |
| Myelin | CNS myelin = glial cell (oligodendrocyte), NOT Schwann cell. |
| Neurotransmitters | They BIND receptors — they do NOT enter the post-synaptic neuron. |
| Adrenaline | In a question, adrenaline/noradrenaline = the HORMONE; norepinephrine = neurotransmitter. |
| Brainstem | Medulla + pons + midbrain. |
| Cortex vs. cerebrum | Cortex = outer layer OF the cerebrum; cerebrum = the whole structure. |
| "50% genetic" | Refers to individual differences, not your trait. |
| Bimodal | Two peaks (textbook concept, may not be covered in class). |
| Standard deviation | AVERAGE distance of all data points from the mean. |
| Reliability | Consistently replicated — memorize it; the name misleads. |
| Consent | Informed consent → informed ASSENT for minors. |
| MDMA | Appears under BOTH stimulants and hallucinogens. |

## Appendix B — Rapid Self-Check

| **Question** | **Answer** |
|---|---|
| Stage with sleep spindles? | NREM-2 |
| Sense that skips the thalamus? | Smell |
| "Gorilla" experiment? | Inattentional blindness |
| Weber's Law = constant ____? | percentage |
| Sudden "Aha!"? | Insight |
| Updating a schema itself? | Accommodation |
| Blindsight patient walking the hallway? | Eyes work, awareness blind (dual processing) |
| Brain wave of deep sleep? | Delta |
| Extra REM after deprivation? | REM rebound |
| Rubbing an injury hurts less? | Gate-control theory |
| Seeing a green after-image? | Opponent-process theory |
| High pitches? Low pitches? | Place theory · Frequency theory |
| Lights blinking in sequence? | Phi phenomenon |
| Movies / animation? | Stroboscopic movement |
| Range of the correlation coefficient? | −1.00 to +1.00 |
